title: Phytochemical Profiling, Antioxidant and Antimicrobial Activities of Rosa damascena Extracts: Influence of Extraction Solvent and Application in a Cosmetic Emulsion
content: Rosa damascena Mill. is widely recognized for its pharmacological and cosmetic value, primarily derived from bioactive polyphenols and volatile monoterpenes. This study evaluated the phytochemical, antioxidant, and antimicrobial properties of nine distinct R. damascena preparations (D1–D9), encompassing distillation hydrosols, essential oil, fresh petal juice, and dried petal extracts obtained with solvents spanning a gradient of polarities (water, methanol, acetone, ethyl acetate, and n-hexane). Phytochemical profiling and antioxidant capacity were determined using total phenolic content (TPC), ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP), and DPPH free-radical scavenging assays, supported by targeted LC-ESI/MS metabolite analysis. Solvent polarity significantly governed phenolic recovery and antioxidant potential. Polar extracts displayed pronounced bioactivity, with acetone (D7) and aqueous (D6) petal extracts yielding the highest total phenolic contents (1890.28 and 1620.85 mg GAE/L, respectively), while methanolic (D5) and aqueous (D6) extracts showed the highest reducing capacities (FRAP: 7625.55 and 7045.12 mM FeSO4 eq.) and strongest radical scavenging activity (IC50 = 1.61 and 1.72 mg/mL}. Conversely, rose waters (D1, D2) and n-hexane extract (D9) demonstrated minimal reducing power and radical scavenging capacity. LC-ESI/MS profiling confirmed substantial concentrations of hydrophilic phenolics in the aqueous extract—notably diosmin (11.89 ppm) and gallic acid (10.82 ppm)—alongside key flavonols, phenolic acids, and anthocyanins across polar preparations. An experimental oil-in-water (O/W) cosmetic emulsion formulated with 2.5% (w/w) R. damascena essential oil effectively retained concentration-dependent DPPH radical scavenging activity. Antimicrobial screening revealed that the 50% ethanol petal extract possessed broad-spectrum microbicidal action, inhibiting Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and Candida albicans with a minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 2.5% (w/v), and demonstrating strong zone inhibition against C. albicans (22.67 mm) and S. aureus (15.00 mm) in agar diffusion assays. Overall, these findings highlight the critical role of solvent polarity in optimizing bioactive extraction and demonstrate the utility of R. damascena extracts and essential oil as multifunctional active ingredients in cosmetic formulations.
